title: Online Auction System — LLD
summary: Real-time competitive bidding: deterministic bid ordering under concurrency, anti-snipe timing, and proxy bidding that raises your bid automatically without exposing your true max.

slides.markdown:
"Design an eBay-style live auction" is the hardest concurrency problem in this group, because unlike a seat or a room, there's no fixed inventory to protect — the contested resource is **the current highest bid itself**, and every bid changes it.

The design has to answer three things simultaneously: which of two near-simultaneous bids wins deterministically, how proxy (automatic) bidding raises your bid without revealing your true maximum to competitors, and how a last-second bid ("sniping") is prevented from unfairly ending the auction before others can respond.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: what's in scope, what isn't
slides.markdown:
**In scope:** sellers create listings with a starting price and an end time; bidders place bids (manual or proxy/auto-bid up to a max); the system determines the current highest bid and, at auction close, the winner; anti-sniping extension logic.

**Explicitly out of scope:** payment settlement, escrow, and shipping/fulfillment mechanics — assume a `PaymentService` handles the winner's charge as a black box once a winner is determined.

The interview payoff is concentrated entirely in bid concurrency and timing — spending time on listing CRUD or payment flow instead is a scoping mistake at this level.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Listing, Bid, Auction, Bidder, ProxyBid
slides.markdown:
`Listing` describes the item and starting price; `Auction` is the live, time-bound process wrapping a listing — it's `Auction`, not `Listing`, that owns bid state and the end time, since the same listing concept could in principle be re-auctioned.

Every placed `Bid` is an immutable, timestamped record — bids are never edited or deleted, only superseded by a newer one, which is what makes the bid history trustworthy for dispute resolution.

`ProxyBid` is a distinct entity from `Bid`: it stores a bidder's private maximum and generates real `Bid`s automatically on the bidder's behalf as competing bids come in, up to that maximum — the max itself is never exposed as a `Bid`.

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: two bids arriving in the same instant
slides.markdown:
Two bidders submit $105 within the same few milliseconds on a $100 auction. Both look valid against a stale read of "current high bid is $100" — exactly the same race shape as seat holding and room inventory, but here the resource being contended isn't a fixed slot, it's a single mutable number that every bid both reads and updates.

The fix is the same family as before: serialize access to that number, either with a row lock held for the whole check-and-write (as in the code above) or an atomic compare-and-swap on `currentHighBid` with a version check, so only one of the two $105 bids can actually win the write. The loser's bid is rejected outright — not queued, not silently dropped — with a clear "someone else bid first" response naming the new current high bid.

What makes this the hardest version of the pattern in this group: unlike a seat or room count, there's no natural batching or pre-check that avoids the write — every single bid must go through this exact serialized path.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: proxy/auto-bidding without exposing your max
Compare: hard close time vs anti-snipe extension window
slides.markdown:
| | Hard close time | Anti-snipe extension |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior at end time | Auction ends exactly on schedule, no exceptions | A late bid within the closing window extends the end time |
| Vulnerability to sniping | High — a bid placed at the last second wins unopposed | Low — snipers just trigger another round instead of winning silently |
| Predictability of end time | Fully predictable in advance | Can extend indefinitely if bids keep arriving |
| Fairness perception | Rewards last-second timing over true willingness to pay | Better reflects genuine highest willingness to pay |

**How to decide:** a hard close is simpler and fine for low-stakes listings; anti-snipe extension is worth the added complexity whenever the item's value makes last-second sniping likely, which is most competitive auctions.

slides.sectionTitle: Modeling outbid notification as an Observer, not a poll
slides.markdown:
When a new high bid lands, every bidder who's now been outbid needs to know — but having each bidder's client poll "am I still winning?" every few seconds wastes requests and still leaves a notification lag.

Modeling `Auction` as a subject that bidders' notification handlers observe means `placeBid` fires an `outbid` event exactly once, at the moment it happens, to exactly the bidders affected — no polling, no wasted requests, and the notification is as close to instant as the event pipeline allows. This is the Observer pattern: bidders subscribe to an auction's bid events instead of the auction (or its notification code) needing to know who to individually push to ahead of time.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: determining the winner by re-scanning the entire bid history
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To find the winner at close, scan all of an auction's bids and pick the maximum — the bid table has everything, so just query it."

**Why it's wrong:** for a popular listing with thousands of bids (proxy bidding alone can generate many automatic counter-bids), re-scanning the full history at close is needless work for information the system already knew the entire time it was tracking `currentHighBid` incrementally, bid by bid.

**Correct model:** `Auction.currentHighBid` (and the bidder who placed it) is maintained incrementally on every accepted bid, exactly as shown in the `placeBid` code — closing the auction just reads that already-current field. A full bid-history scan should exist only for audits and disputes, never on the hot path of determining who won.
